```{r setup}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(maps)    # maps!
library(sf)      # maps!
library(stars)   # rasters!
library(ggrepel) # labelling
```

## Introduction

This week we're looking at spatial data with emphasis on mapping. We'll be looking at polygon maps, simple features, coordinate reference systems and raster data.

## Polygons!

We'll start with the easiest way to specify map data: using polygons. The `map_data()` function of `ggplot2` contains some maps (via the `maps` package) that isn't very up to date or high resolution but is nonetheless available to us nice and easily.

And it contains a map of Aotearoa/NZ! We can grab it using:

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
nz <- map_data("nz")
head(nz)
```

Notice this is quite simple: we have a data frame with longitude (x), latitude (y), group (as there are multiple islands to draw), order (the order the points should be drawn in) region and subregion.

To draw this, we can treat it like a standard data frame and use the geometries we're used to, such as `geom_point()`:

```{r my first map}
ggplot(nz) +
  aes(x=long, y=lat) +
  geom_point()
```

TADA! New Zealand! Or perhaps quite a squashed version thereof as the scale for latitude and longitude are different. We can make it look a bit prettier by using `coord_sf()` which for now will just ensure lat and long are what you might expect, given their location on the planet

### Try yourself

1. Add `coord_sf()` to the above chart to get the coordinates looking right.

```{r}
ggplot(data=nz) +
  aes(x=long, y=lat) +
  geom_point() +
  coord_sf()
```

2. Try switching to `geom_polygon()` instead of `geom_point()`. You should get something approximately correct!

```{r}
ggplot(data = nz) +
  aes(x=long, y=lat) +
  geom_polygon() +
  coord_sf()
```


3. The extra trick you need is there are multiple islands which are described using separate polygons: `geom_polygon` is currently just rendering them all as one polygon so joining them all up. If you add `group=group` (noting the `group` column in `nz`) then you should get something better.

```{r}
ggplot(data = nz) +
  aes(x=long, y=lat, group=group) +
  geom_polygon() +
  coord_sf()
```

4. Try playing with `fill` and `colour`. e.g. you could set them directly or map them to the `region` column.

```{r}
ggplot(data = nz) +
  aes(x=long, y=lat, group=group) +
  geom_polygon(fill='lightgreen', colour = 'black', linewidth=0.2) +
  coord_sf()
```

The problem with the above is that it's quite basic: each shape or island is described by just one polygon. This is fine in many cases, but often you might want more. e.g. we might want Lake Taupō to be rendered correctly: that's a polygon within a polygon (i.e. the land has a hole in it) so things can get pretty complicated pretty quickly.

The other advantage of simple lat/long data is it's really easy to plot locations on such a map if we assume that longitude and latitude are *planar*: i.e. they're just like typical x and y and can treat it as if the landscape was flat. Ofcourse this isn't true: they actually lie on some sort of slightly squashed sphere. Nonetheless, for many things we'll want to pretend maps are flat (e.g. for printing on paper and putting in an atlas, or for many statistical analyses), even when they're not!

## Simple features

Most map data that is available don't use the simple lat/long data format. Instead maps are usually encoded using "simple features", a standard from the Open Geospatial Consortium. We can work with simple features data using the `sf` package, and `geom_sf()` or `coord_sf()` can be used in ggplot2 to utilise these data.

Continuing with our Aotearoa/NZ theme let's load some simple features data for NZ that's stored in an sqlite database.

```{r}
# this should just work (tm)
nz <- read_sf("https://www.massey.ac.nz/~jcmarsha/data/nz_map/sa3_data.sqlite")

# in case it doesn't, you can download the maps data directly with the below, you can download using:
#download.file("https://www.massey.ac.nz/~jcmarsha/data/nz_map/sa3_data.sqlite", dest="sa3_data.sqlite")
#nz <- read_sf("sa3_data.sqlite")
nz
```

Notice we have a data frame object that has a few extras: it has a `GEOMETRY` column that contains a bunch of `sfc_MULTIPOLYGON`'s as well as some additional information about the geometry (bounding box, projected coordinate reference system etc).

We can chart this with `geom_sf()` which automatically uses the projected coordinate reference system (so it plots on a non-planar set of axes):

```{r}
ggplot(nz) +
  geom_sf()
```

Note that this works even when we don't specify any aesthetics. This is because the `geometry` aesthetic is only used by `geom_sf()` and nothing else, so you don't need to specify it (except if your sf has two geometry columns).

### Try yourself

1. Explore changing the chart with `fill`, `colour`, `linewidth` etc.

```{r}
ggplot(data=nz) +
  geom_sf(fill='lightgreen', colour='purple', linewidth=0.1)
```

```{r}
ggplot(data=nz) +
  aes(fill=mean_hours_worked) +
  geom_sf(linewidth=0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c()
```

2. Try filtering the data to the Auckland territorial authority and then plot.

```{r}
nz |>
  filter(territorial_authority == "Auckland") |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(fill=mean_hours_worked) +
  geom_sf()
```

3. Another way to zoom in is to use a bounding box (xlim/ylim) to `coord_sf()`. To get an appropriate bounding box for Auckland, we can use `nz |> filter(territorial_authority == "Auckland") |> st_bbox()`. We can then apply that bounding box to the entire `nz` map by using `coord_sf()`. Try that!

```{r}
nz |>
  filter(territorial_authority == "Auckland") |>
  st_bbox()

boundary <- list(x=c(1704086, 1828990),
                y=c(5871395, 6025308))

nz |>
#  filter(territorial_authority == "Auckland") |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(fill=mean_hours_worked) +
  geom_sf() +
  coord_sf(xlim = boundary$x, ylim=boundary$y)
```

4. The bounding box you found is coordinates that are referenced in metres rather than long/lat that are what ends up on the chart. Try plotting the chart in metres by adding `datum=NULL` to `coord_sf()`.

```{r}
ggplot(data = nz) +
  geom_sf() +
  coord_sf(datum=NULL)
```

5. Try producing a zoomed in map of Wellington by finding an appropriate boundary box.

```{r}
well_bound <- list(x=c(1730000, 1770000),
                   y=c(5410000, 5460000))
ggplot(nz) +
  geom_sf() +
  coord_sf(xlim=well_bound$x,
           ylim=well_bound$y)
```

## Combining regions

The above map has lots of small regions (statistical area level 3). We might want a higher level, which are available to us in the data as `territorial_authority` for example. We can combine the usual `dplyr` grouping tools with spatial tools from `sf` such as `st_union()`.

```{r}
ta_nz <- nz |> group_by(territorial_authority, regional_council) |>
  summarise(geometry = st_union(GEOMETRY))
ta_nz # combined geometry
ggplot(ta_nz) +
  geom_sf()

# zoom in on wellington
ggplot(ta_nz) +
  geom_sf() +
  coord_sf(xlim=well_bound$x,
           ylim=well_bound$y)
```

## Try yourself

1. Combine the sa3 level data by regional council and plot that, coloured by council.

```{r}
reg_nz <- nz |> group_by(regional_council) |> summarise() # automatically applies st_union() to the GEOMETRY column

ggplot(data=reg_nz) +
  aes(fill = regional_council) +
  geom_sf()
```

2. Add the appropriate `guides()` line to turn off the guide.

```{r}
ggplot(data=reg_nz) +
  aes(fill = regional_council) +
  geom_sf() +
  guides(fill='none')
```

## Labelling maps

It's often useful to add a label to each region on a map. To illustrate this, let's zoom into the middle of Palmerston North:

```{r}
palmy_bb <- list(x=c(1816000, 1828000), y=c(5523000, 5533000)) # magic bounding box
nz |> filter(territorial_authority == "Palmerston North City") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(mapping=aes(fill = sa3_name)) +
  coord_sf(xlim = palmy_bb$x, ylim=palmy_bb$y) +
  geom_sf_label(mapping=aes(label=sa3_name), size=3) +
  guides(fill = 'none')
```

Like all annotation, it can be tricky to not have overlapping labels.

### Try yourself

1. Investigate the `geom_label_repel()` function using `stat = "sf_coordinates"` from the `ggrepel` package. You may have to explicitly provide `geometry=geometry` to `aes()`.

```{r}
nz |> filter(territorial_authority == "Palmerston North City") |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(geometry = GEOMETRY) +
  geom_sf(mapping=aes(fill = sa3_name)) +
  coord_sf(xlim = palmy_bb$x, ylim=palmy_bb$y) +
  geom_label_repel(mapping=aes(label=sa3_name), stat = "sf_coordinates", size=3) +
  guides(fill = 'none')
```

2. Investigate the various aesthetic options for the labels (fill, alpha, colour, linewidth, padding, radius etc).

```{r}
nz |> filter(territorial_authority == "Palmerston North City") |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(geometry = GEOMETRY) +
  geom_sf(mapping=aes(fill = sa3_name)) +
  coord_sf(xlim = palmy_bb$x, ylim=palmy_bb$y) +
  geom_label_repel(mapping=aes(label=sa3_name), stat = "sf_coordinates", size=3,
                   fill='brown', label.r=0.4, alpha=0.5) +
  guides(fill = 'none')
```


## Adding other geometries

You can add other geometries onto a map as well: there's nothing particularly special about it. The trick is they have to use the same coordinate system. Our map uses the NZGD2000 map grid which is in northing/easting. As long as our points are in the same x,y northing/easting scale and origin we'll be fine.

e.g. We have some data from schools which has longitude/latitude as well as NZGD2000 coordinates:

```{r}
schools <- read_csv("https://www.massey.ac.nz/~jcmarsha/data/nz_map/schools.csv")
schools
```

Plotting this is straight-forward with `geom_point()` noting that we specify the `data` parameter:

```{r}
ggplot(nz) +
  geom_sf() +
  geom_point(data=schools, aes(x=x, y=y), col='purple', alpha=0.3, size=1)
```

Things are a bit trickier if they're not in the same coordinates though!

## Coordinate reference systems

The planet is not flat. It's not a sphere either. Instead it's some weird ellipisoid thing.

So when we have map data we have alongside it a set of assumptions about the shape of the earth and those assumptions vary depending on the data (location, scope etc). This is the *geodetic datum*. It normally defines the origin, shape and scope.

In addition, we have the problem of drawing the map onto "paper" (or a plane). This inevitably involves distortion or cutting of the map. This is the job of the *map projection*.

The combination of *geodetic datum* and *projection* make up the coordinate reference system or CRS:

```{r}
st_crs(nz)
```

Most of this is a *WKT* (well-known text) string that provides all the information to describe the CRS. It's verbose, but regularly used ones are assigned an *EPSG code* which in this case is 2193.

We can control the CRS using `coord_sf()`. e.g: to use WGS84 like google maps does:

```{r}
ggplot(nz) +
  geom_sf() + coord_sf(crs=st_crs("WGS84"))
```

## Using longitude/latitude

Often point data for a map comes in longitude/latitude rather than whatever coordinate system the map uses (often an easting/northing pair).

It would be convenient if we could just plot long/lat directly on top of a map without having to deal with coordinate reference transformation.

We can do this in some cases by utilising the `default_crs` option of `coord_crs`. This is the CRS to use for all non-SF data (like points).

### Try yourself

1. Set `default_crs=st_crs("WGS84")` in `coord_sf()` and then use `long` and `lat` for the x, y aesthetics in `geom_point()` for the schools.

```{r}
ggplot(data=nz) +
  geom_sf() +
  geom_point(data=schools, aes(x=long, y=lat), alpha=0.3, col='steelblue') +
  coord_sf(default_crs = st_crs("WGS84"))
```


The above should have worked fine. Let's try it again, but this time with this dataset which includes the schools in the Chatham/Pitt Islands:

```{r}
schools_ci <- read_csv("https://www.massey.ac.nz/~jcmarsha/data/nz_map/schools_ci.csv")
ggplot(nz) +
  geom_sf() +
  geom_point(data=schools_ci, aes(x=long, y=lat), col='purple', alpha=0.3, size=1) + coord_sf(default_crs=st_crs("WGS84"))
```

Welcome to NZ where the Chathams are technically in the other hemisphere. Aren't maps fun! :)

One way to deal with this (there are many!) is to convert the schools_ci data into a simple features object and set the geometry and coordinate system for it. e.g. for lat/long data we can use `st_as_sf()` to convert to `sf` then use "WGS84" as the CRS:

```{r}
schools_sf <- schools_ci |> st_as_sf(coords = c("long", "lat")) |>
  st_set_crs("WGS84")

schools_sf
```

### Try yourself

1. Use the `schools_sf` to add the school points to a map of `nz` with `geom_sf(data=schools_sf)`.

```{r}
ggplot(data=nz) +
  geom_sf() +
  geom_sf(data=schools_sf, alpha=0.2, col='red')
```

## Working with sf data

It's important to be able to combine or break down the `geometry` data in an `sf` data frame sometimes.

For example, suppose we wish to produce a map of Rangitoto and Motutapu islands in Auckland.

We find these are in the `Hibiscus and Bays Rural` SA3:

```{r}
bb_auckland <- list(x=c(1745000, 1795000), y=c(5910000, 5940000))
nz |> filter(territorial_authority == "Auckland") |>
  mutate(highlight = sa3_name == "Hibiscus and Bays Rural") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(mapping=aes(fill=highlight)) +
  coord_sf(xlim=bb_auckland$x, ylim=bb_auckland$y) +
  guides(fill='none')
```

If we take a look at the geometry for this we see it's a `sfc_MULTIPOLYGON`:

```{r}
hibiscus <- nz |> filter(sa3_name == "Hibiscus and Bays Rural")
hibiscus |> relocate(GEOMETRY) # relocate pulls the column left so we can see it easier
```

We can use `st_cast()` to convert this to it's constituent polygons:

```{r}
hibiscus |> st_cast(to="POLYGON") |>
  rowid_to_column('polygon') |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf() +
  geom_sf_label(mapping=aes(label=polygon))
```

We see that Rangitoto is row 1 and Motutapu is row 10, so we can grab and label these accordingly:

```{r}
rangitoto_motutapu <- hibiscus |> st_cast(to="POLYGON") |>
  slice(c(1, 10)) |>
  mutate(label = c("Rangitoto", "Motutapu"))

ggplot(rangitoto_motutapu) +
  geom_sf() +
  geom_sf_label(mapping=aes(label=label))
```

### Try yourself

1. Create a map of Mou Waho, one of the relatively small number of islands that are in lakes on an island that contain a lake (recursive lakes!). Look this up on a map online so you can see where it is relative to the surroundings. Then filter the data down to the appropriate `sa3`, break down the geometry and do a map of only Mou Waho.

```{r}
wanaka <- nz |>
  filter(str_detect(sa3_name, "Wānaka Outer"))

wanaka_split <- wanaka |> st_cast(to="POLYGON") |>
  rowid_to_column('polygon')

wanaka_split |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(fill=as.factor(polygon)) +
  geom_sf() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette='Accent') # we want number 5

mou_waho <- wanaka_split |>
  filter(polygon == 5) # Mou Waho

# plot it:
ggplot(data=mou_waho) +
  geom_sf()
```

## Raster data

The other main type of mapping data are raster data: essentially an area that is tiled with a grid and some variable is represented as a value at each grid location. The data are usually in the form of an **image** with pixels representing the tiles. The grids may be rectangular tiles, but they could also be non-rectangular, or projected onto the globe. A common format is GeoTIFF which is basically a TIFF with additional metadata describing the CRS and extent of the tiled area.

```{r}
oz_cloud <- read_stars("https://www.massey.ac.nz/~jcmarsha/data/nz_map/aussie_cloud.tif")

# in case it doesn't, you can download the maps data directly with the below, you can download using:
#download.file("https://www.massey.ac.nz/~jcmarsha/data/nz_map/aussie_cloud.tif", dest="aussie_cloud.tif")
#oz_cloud <- read_stars("aussie_cloud.tif")
ggplot() + geom_stars(data=oz_cloud) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "black", high = "white")
```

```{r}
st_crs(oz_cloud)
nz3 <- nz |> st_transform(crs = st_crs(oz_cloud))

ggplot() + 
  geom_stars(data = oz_cloud, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_sf(data = nz3, fill = NA, color = "white", linewidth=0.1) + 
  coord_sf() + 
  theme_void() + 
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "black", high = "white")
```

Ah, a map technically with New Zealand!

We also have data from Manaaki Whenua Landcare Research on proportion of forestry cover in New Zealand:

```{r}
forest <- read_stars("https://www.massey.ac.nz/~jcmarsha/data/nz_map/forest.tif")
# in case it doesn't, you can download the maps data directly with the below, you can download using:
#download.file("https://www.massey.ac.nz/~jcmarsha/data/nz_map/forest.tif", dest="forest.tif")
#forest <- read_stars("forest.tif")
forest
```

These data are already referenced in NZGD2000/NZTM2000 so no need to transform our `nz` data to the same CRS.

## Try yourself

1. Try charting the `forest` data on the `nz` map.

```{r}
# Method one is put the map on top of the raster so you can see the outline
ggplot(nz) +
  geom_stars(data=forest) +
  geom_sf(fill='transparent')

# Method 2 is the other way around, using `na.value` to be transparent
ggplot(nz) +
  geom_sf(fill='transparent') +
  geom_stars(data=forest) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option='plasma', na.value='transparent')
```

2. Investigate a spatial join of the forest data with the `nz` map to summarise the proportion of forestry cover by `sa3`. See the lecture material for how to do this!

```{r}
# convert our raster to a simple features with the same CRS as nz
forest_sf <- forest |> st_as_sf() |> st_transform(st_crs(nz))
nz_cover <- nz |> st_join(forest_sf) |>
  group_by(sa3, sa3_name, territorial_authority, regional_council) |>
  summarise(prop_forest = mean(forest.tif, na.rm=TRUE))
nz_cover
```

3. Produce a chart of forestry cover in the South Island. The easiest way to get the south island only might be to use `xlim`, `ylim` pairs.

```{r}
south_bb <- list(x=c(1100000, 1720000),
                 y=c(4750000, 5520000))

nz_cover |> replace_na(replace=list(prop_forest = 0)) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(fill=prop_forest) +
  geom_sf() +
  coord_sf(xlim=south_bb$x, ylim=south_bb$y) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c()
```


4. Add suitable labelling etc to this map. You might want to investigate the `ggspatial` package for adding a north symbols or scales to the map.

```{r}
library(ggspatial)
nz_cover |> replace_na(replace=list(prop_forest = 0)) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(fill=prop_forest) +
  geom_sf() +
  coord_sf(xlim=south_bb$x, ylim=south_bb$y) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(label = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(fill='Forest coverage') +
  annotation_north_arrow(which_north = "true", location='tl',
                         height=unit(1, 'cm'), width=unit(1, 'cm'),
                         style = north_arrow_nautical)
```
